content: Antipsychotic medications are the cornerstone of treatment for schizophrenia. Clinical guidelines suggest that there is no significant difference in efficacy among various antipsychotic drugs. However, clinicians often perceive low-potency antipsychotics as less effective compared to high-potency agents, and these two classes of drugs also differ in their side effect profiles. This review specifically evaluated the effects of the high-potency antipsychotic fluphenazine in comparison to low-potency first-generation antipsychotics in individuals with schizophrenia. The review included seven randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 1,567 participants. The sample sizes of the individual studies ranged from 40 to 438 participants. The quality of reporting for randomization, allocation, and blinding procedures was generally poor. In terms of treatment response, there was no significant difference between fluphenazine and low-potency antipsychotics. Approximately 55% of participants in both groups responded to treatment (2 RCTs, n = 105, risk ratio [RR] 1.06, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.75 to 1.50, moderate-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no significant difference in treatment acceptability, as indicated by the proportion of participants who discontinued the studies for any reason (fluphenazine 36%, low-potency antipsychotics 36%, 6 RCTs, n = 1,532, RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.14, moderate-quality evidence). Regarding adverse effects, there was no significant difference in the overall number of participants experiencing at least one adverse event (fluphenazine 70%, low-potency antipsychotics 88%, 1 RCT, n = 65, RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.07, moderate-quality evidence). However, movement disorders were significantly more common in the fluphenazine group. For example, at least one movement disorder occurred in 15% of participants treated with fluphenazine compared to 10% in the low-potency antipsychotic group (3 RCTs, n = 971, RR 2.11, 95% CI 1.41 to 3.15, low-quality evidence). Specific movement-related adverse effects such as akathisia (15% vs. 6%, 5 RCTs, n = 1,209, RR 2.28, 95% CI 1.58 to 3.28), dystonia (5% vs. 2%, 4 RCTs, n = 1,309, RR 2.66, 95% CI 1.25 to 5.64), loss of associated movement (20% vs. 2%, 1 RCT, n = 338, RR 11.15, 95% CI 3.95 to 31.47), rigor (27% vs. 12%, 2 RCTs, n = 403, RR 2.18, 95% CI 1.20 to 3.97), and tremor (15% vs. 6%, 2 RCTs, n = 403, RR 2.53, 95% CI 1.37 to 4.68) were significantly more frequent in the fluphenazine group. Conversely, low-potency antipsychotics were associated with significantly higher rates of sedation (64% vs. 20%, 1 RCT, n = 65, RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.77, high-quality evidence). Other adverse effects such as dizziness (8% vs. 17%, 4 RCTs, n = 1,051, RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.73), drowsiness (18% vs. 25%, 3 RCTs, n = 986, RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.86), dry mouth (11% vs. 18%, 4 RCTs, n = 1,051, RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.89), nausea (4% vs. 15%, 3 RCTs, n = 986, RR 0.25, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.45), and vomiting (3% vs. 8%, 3 RCTs, n = 986, RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.18 to 0.72) were significantly more common in the low-potency antipsychotic group, favoring fluphenazine for these outcomes. No data were available regarding mortality or quality of life outcomes. The primary findings were consistent across subgroup and sensitivity analyses. In conclusion, the evidence does not demonstrate a clear difference in efficacy between fluphenazine and low-potency antipsychotics for the treatment of schizophrenia. However, the adverse effect profiles of these drugs differ significantly, with fluphenazine being associated with more movement disorders and low-potency antipsychotics causing more sedation and other side effects. The limited number of studies and their moderate quality highlight the need for further research to better understand the relative benefits and risks of these medications.
